content: Drug delivery systems transport pharmaceutical compounds to specific body locations at controlled rates to optimize therapeutic effects while minimizing side effects. The pharmacokinetic processes of ADMEâabsorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretionâgovern a drug's journey through the body. Absorption occurs when drugs enter the bloodstream through various routes: oral medications pass through gastrointestinal tract membranes; intravenous delivery provides direct bloodstream access; transdermal patches allow absorption through skin; and inhalation enables rapid absorption through lung alveoli. Once in circulation, distribution transports drugs throughout the body, with factors like blood flow, protein binding, and tissue permeability affecting drug concentration at different sites. Biological barriers present significant challenges: the blood-brain barrier protects the central nervous system from many substances; the placental barrier filters materials between maternal and fetal circulation; and cellular membranes selectively control molecule entry based on size, charge, and lipid solubility. Advanced delivery systems overcome these challenges through various mechanisms: liposomes (phospholipid vesicles) encapsulate drugs to improve stability and targeting; nanoparticles provide controlled release and can be functionalized with targeting molecules; implantable devices deliver drugs at specific sites over extended periods; and modified-release formulations control dissolution rates for optimal blood concentrations. Drug targeting approaches include passive targeting (exploiting physiological features like enhanced permeability in tumor vasculature), active targeting (using ligands that bind specific cell receptors), and physical targeting (applying external forces like magnetic fields to direct drug-carrying particles). Controlled-release mechanisms include diffusion-controlled systems where drugs pass through polymer matrices; chemically-controlled systems where drug release follows polymer degradation; and stimuli-responsive systems that release drugs in response to specific triggers like pH changes, temperature, or externally applied signals.

scenario.title: Therapeutic Transport Network
scenario.content: Students manage a delivery system where drug packages must navigate from administration sites to target organs via the circulatory system. The simulation allows students to select various drug formulations, delivery routes, and targeting mechanisms, then observe how these choices affect drug distribution, efficacy, and side effects. The system visualizes pharmacokinetic processes as packages move through body compartments, encountering barriers, binding to proteins, undergoing metabolism, and reaching receptors. Students can manipulate drug properties like molecular size, solubility, and stability to observe their impact on delivery success. Interactive tools demonstrate advanced delivery technologies including liposomes, nanoparticles, and controlled-release systems. Challenge scenarios require students to design optimal delivery strategies for different therapeutic needsâtreating brain disorders, targeting specific cell types, or maintaining consistent drug levels over timeâteaching principles of pharmaceutical science through an engaging logistics metaphor.

hypothesis.description: Students will design drug delivery strategies by analyzing how pharmaceutical compounds move through biological systems. They will predict how drug properties and delivery methods affect distribution patterns and therapeutic outcomes, and develop targeted approaches that maximize efficacy while minimizing side effects.
